title: The Idalion Tablet
bodyHtml:
In 1850, a farmer from a village in Cyprus discovered a tablet dating from the 5th century BCE, which recorded an endowment from the city of Idalion to a family of physicians. Now known as the Idalion Tablet, this document was of enormous importance for the decipherment of the Cypriot script in which it was written. The tablet is in the Cypriot dialect of ancient Greek.

Here is a portion of the inscription, with a transliteration below:

ote ta ptolin edalion kateworgon madoi kas ketiēwes i tōi philokuprōn wetei tō onasagorau basileus stasikupros kas ha ptolis edaliēwes anōgon onasilon tononasikuprōn toniyatēran kas tos kasignētos iyasthai tos athrōpos tos i tai makhai ikhimamenos aneu misthōn

H1. Here are four other words from the Idalion Tablet. Write them in the Cypriot script.

helei     athanas     kathethiyan     dowenai

H2. Here is the English translation of this section of the text:

“When the Medes and the Kitions subdued the city of Idalion in the year of Philokypros son of Onasagoras, King Stasikypros and the city of the Idalians instructed Onasion the son of Onasikypros the physician, and his brothers, to heal the men wounded in the battle, without a fee.”

What are the Cypriot Greek for (a) and, (b) king, (c) instructed? Write them in the Cypriot script.

assets.alt: Five lines of the Idalion Tablet inscription written in the Cypriot syllabary

questions.partPrompt: Here are four other words from the Idalion Tablet. Write each one in the Cypriot script. Because the syllabary cannot be typed here, give the sign-by-sign spelling instead: one syllable per sign, separated by hyphens. For example, the first word of the text, ote, is spelled o-te (two signs).

Using the English translation, work out the Cypriot Greek word for each meaning below and write it in the Cypriot script. As in H1, give the sign-by-sign spelling: one syllable per sign, separated by hyphens.

hints.text: Count things. The inscription has far fewer signs than the transliteration has letters, so each sign cannot be a single letter. Compare the number of signs in a line with the syllables of the words, and remember that this inscription runs from right to left.

Each sign stands for a vowel on its own or a consonant plus a vowel, so a word like ma-to-i needs three signs. That means the script must do something with sounds that do not fit the pattern. Look for these habits: h is simply not written, long and short vowels share signs, and voiced and aspirated stops (d, b, g, th, ph, kh) share signs with plain t, p, k. A consonant with no vowel after it borrows one: at the end of a word it borrows e, and inside a cluster it repeats the vowel of the neighbouring syllable.

Try a word from the passage itself. In kateworgon the syllables ka and te are easy, but the cluster rg and the final n are not. The r borrows the vowel of the syllable that follows it, g is written like k, and the final n borrows e, so the spelling comes out as six signs: ka-te-wo-ro-ko-ne. Apply exactly the same reasoning to the words you are asked about.

explanationHtml:
Step 1: what kind of script is this?

The transliteration under the picture is long — dozens of letters — but each line of the inscription has only about thirty signs. So the signs cannot be letters. In fact the Cypriot script is a syllabary: every sign stands for a whole syllable, and the syllables come in just two shapes, a vowel alone (a, e, i, o, u) or a consonant plus a vowel (ka, te, mi, po...). The inscription is written from right to left, which is why the sign groups line up with the transliteration in reverse.

A good way to check this is with a short word. madoi “witnesses” has five letters but only three syllables, ma-do-i, and indeed it takes three signs.

Step 2: the spelling habits of the syllabary

Greek has sounds that do not fit a simple set of consonant-plus-vowel signs, so the syllabary has fixed tricks for them. Each one can be spotted in the passage:

  • h is not written at all. The text has ha ptolis “and the city,” and the sign group for it begins with plain a: a-po-to-li-se.
  • Long vowels are written like short ones. tōi uses the ordinary to sign; anōgon uses the ordinary no sign.
  • Voiced and aspirated stops share signs with the plain voiceless ones. d is written like t, b like p, g like k, and th, ph, kh like t, p, k. That is why the city called Idalion in English appears here as edalion and is spelled with t signs, e-ta-li-o-ne, and why philokuprōn starts with the pi sign.
  • A word-final consonant borrows the vowel e. Greek words end in -s or -n, and the syllabary writes these with the se and ne signs: kas is ka-se, ptolin ends in ne.
  • Inside a cluster, a consonant with no vowel of its own repeats a neighbour's vowel. Usually it copies the following vowel: ptolin is po-to-li-ne (the p takes o from the next syllable), kasignētos is ka-si-ke-ne-to-se. An s standing before another consonant copies the vowel before it instead: misthōn is mi-si-to-ne.
  • The sound y has its own sign, ya. toniyatēran is to-ni-ya-te-ra-ne.

Step 3: spelling the four words of H1

  • helei: drop the h, and the rest is e-le-i — three signs.
  • athanas: a, then th written like t (ta), then na, then the final s written with se: four signs.
  • kathethiyan: ka, the (written te), thi (written ti), ya with the special y sign, and the final n written ne: five signs.
  • dowenai: d is written like t, so do becomes the to sign, then we, na, i: four signs.

The official answer sheet draws these in the syllabary itself, right to left; here you write the same signs out one per syllable.

Step 4: reading the translation for H2

Now use the English. “And” shows up three times (the Medes and the Kitions; King Stasikypros and the city; and his brothers), and exactly one Greek word occurs three times in the transliteration: kas. Its spelling follows the final-consonant rule.

“King Stasikypros” in English sits beside basileus stasikupros in Greek, so “king” is basileus. Since b is written like p, the spelling is five signs: pa-si-le-u-se.

“Instructed” is the verb of the sentence “King Stasikypros and the city of the Idalians instructed Onasion...”. In the Greek, the words after kas ha ptolis edaliēwes (“and the city of the Idalians”) and before onasilon (“Onasion”) are anōgon. Writing g like k and ō like o, and giving the final n the vowel e, this comes to four signs: a-no-ko-ne.
